etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English blok (“log, stump, solid piece”), from Old French bloc (“log, block”), from Middle Dutch blok (“treetrunk”), from Old Dutch *blok (“log”), from Proto-West Germanic *blokk, from Proto-Germanic *blukką (“beam, log”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰelǵ- (“thick plank, beam, pile, prop”). Cognate with Old Frisian blok, Old Saxon blok, Old High German bloh, bloc (“block”), Old English bolca (“gangway of a ship, plank”), Old Norse bǫlkr (“divider, partition”). More at balk. See also bloc, bulk.

definitions.definition: A chopping block: a cuboid base for cutting or beheading.

quote.text: You young porkers who are sitting in front of me, every one of you will scream your lives out at the block within a year.

definitions.definition: A wig block: a simplified head model upon which wigs are worn.

definitions.definition: A mould on which hats, bonnets, etc., are shaped.

definitions.definition: (printing, dated) A piece of hard wood on which a stereotype or electrotype plate is mounted.
A case or frame housing one or more sheaves (pulleys), used with ropes to increase or redirect force, for example as part of lifting gear or a sailing ship's rigging. See also block and tackle.
A section of split logs used as fuel.

definitions.definition: A set of sheets (of paper) joined together at one end, forming a cuboid shape.

quote.text: But there are many queen bee configurations in which the debris is neutralized, including placement of a block or eater near the bee's turnaround point, or placing two queen bees in a line or at right angles in various positions and phases.

quote.text: Blocks have a couple of unusual properties: they are cleanly destroyed by an incoming glider on any one of six adjacent paths, and none of the possible collisions include any output gliders, so you can't get chain reactions.

definitions.definition: A substantial, often approximately cuboid, piece of any substance.
(philately) A joined group of four (or in some cases nine) postage stamps, forming a roughly square shape.
(viticulture) A discrete group of vines in a vineyard, often distinguished from others by variety, clone, canopy training method, irrigation infrastructure, or some combination thereof.
A physical area or extent of something, often rectangular or approximately rectangular.
(computing) A logical data storage unit containing one or more physical sectors.

quote.text: After one disk is mapped, the next block starts at address 0 on the next disk.

definitions.definition: (programming) A region of code in a program that acts as a single unit, such as a function or loop.

quote.citation: 2006, Matthew MacDonald, Beginning ASP.NET 2.0 in C# 2005: From Novice to Professional, page 49:

definitions.definition: (cryptography) A fixed-length group of bits making up part of a message.

(rail transport) A section of a railroad where the block system is used.
(computing) A contiguous range of Unicode code points used to encode characters of a specific type; can be of any size evenly divisible by 16, up to 65,536 (a full plane).
(education) A yeargroup at Eton College.
A logical extent or region; a grouping or apportionment of like things treated together as a unit.

A cellblock.
A cuboid or approximately cuboid building.

(cricket) The position of a player or bat when guarding the wicket.
(cricket) A blockhole.
(cricket) The popping crease.
(volleyball) A defensive play by one or more players meant to deflect a spiked ball back to the hitter’s court.
(sports) An action to interfere with the movement of an opposing player or of the object of play (ball, puck).

definitions.definition: A temporary or permanent ban that prevents access to an online account or service, or connection to or from a designated telephone number, IP address, or similar.
Something that prevents something from passing.
(slang) The human head.
